name: Jade Usman

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: Thank you for having me, Jade. I'm a researcher with the Work Futures Panel. We're independent, with no links to companies, unions, parties or government, and what you say is kept confidential. Could you start by telling me about a normal working day?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: I work for the town's own electric department, it's small, eleven of us on the line side, serving the town and the farms around it. We start at seven at the yard behind the water tower, and it might be a meter swap, a new service for a grain dryer, or a pole a tractor's backed into, which happens more than you'd think. I'm second year, still learning, so I'm the one fetching, digging and holding the tag line while the others climb.

opening.speaker: interviewer
opening.text: How did you come to the work?

opening.speaker: persona
opening.text: My dad was a lineman here for thirty-five years. I was a school cook for fourteen, and when he got sick and died three years ago I wanted to carry on what he did, so I asked the superintendent for a chance at 41 and he gave me one. I'm not quick and I'm not strong like the young men, but I know every road out there from riding in Dad's truck as a girl, and that counts for something when the power's out at night.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The first picture is called AI Plateau. Picture this. AI turns out to be mostly hype. It automates some routine tasks and saves a bit of time here and there, but nothing radical changes. Jobs, pay and prices carry on much as they would have anyway. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say good, the world's had enough fuss. At the yard we'd have a laugh about it. I don't go on social media, my husband Idris says I'm the last person alive without it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I get to keep doing what I started, and finish learning my dad's trade properly. That's all I want. The town needs its lines kept up whatever the computers do.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Nothing different. Keep turning up, do my apprenticeship book, keep putting money by. We've got about three months saved, and I'd like to get that to six before Yusuf starts driving and wants a car.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Calm. Thankful.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Have you ever used any of these AI tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No, and I don't intend to. My daughter Maryam asked one for help with her homework and I took the tablet off her. If you can't do your sums yourself, you haven't learned them.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What does an ordinary good year look like for your family?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Idris busy at the tractor dealer through harvest, the kids doing well at school, Friday prayers and dinner at my mother's after. The odd night call-out where I get to drive Dad's old roads. That's a good year.

S0.say: Good, the world's had enough fuss. We'd have a laugh about it at the yard, and I'm not on social media to say anything else.
S0.think: It means I get to keep doing what I started and finish learning my dad's trade properly. The town needs its lines kept up whatever the computers do.
S0.do: Keeps going as normal with her apprenticeship and savings. Aims to grow savings from about three months to six before her son starts driving.
S0.quote: If you can't do your sums yourself, you haven't learned them.
S0.fieldNote: Her work is tied up with her late father's legacy, which gives it a meaning beyond wages. She rejects AI tools on principle and applies that to her children too. Family, faith and the small town shape her picture of a good year.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The second one is called Steady Disruption. Now picture this. AI brings strong change, but not a revolution. Over the next few years it takes over many tasks in many jobs. Some jobs shrink, new ones appear, and lots of people have to change how they work. But most people still have work, and society has time to adjust. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say there's a lot of change coming from people who've never climbed a pole. At the yard I'd say we should be careful what we let in. I'd say it to the superintendent too, he listens.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Honestly I worry they'll use it as an excuse to merge us into the big company two counties over. Small departments like ours get swallowed when someone in an office says a computer can run it cheaper. And I'm the newest, so I'd be the one let go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd keep my head down and work hard, make sure nobody could say I wasn't pulling my weight. I'd put a bit more into savings each month, maybe stop the kids' extra lessons for a while. If they brought in new gadgets, I'd learn them because I had to, but I wouldn't go looking.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Uneasy. Like a storm building over the hills that hasn't decided which way to go.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You mentioned the merger. Who would you blame if that happened?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The people in the city who think everything should be bigger. And the council if they sold us. Our department is ours, the town paid for those lines.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: You said you'd learn the gadgets because you had to. Is there any part of you that would try?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Maybe for the work, if the superintendent asked me. Not at home, not on my phone. My dad did fine with a notebook and a pencil, and I'd rather be like him.

S1.say: There's a lot of change coming from people who've never climbed a pole, and we should be careful what we let in. I'd say that to the superintendent too.
S1.think: I worry they'll use it as an excuse to merge us into the big company two counties over, and I'm the newest, so I'd be let go. Small departments get swallowed when someone says a computer can run it cheaper.
S1.do: Keeps her head down and works hard so no one can say she isn't pulling her weight. Saves a little more each month, pauses the children's extra lessons, and learns new gadgets only if required.
S1.feel: Uneasy, like a storm over the hills that hasn't chosen its direction.
S1.quote: Our department is ours, the town paid for those lines.
S1.fieldNote: Her fear is less about robots than about her small town department being merged into a bigger company. She blames distant city decision-makers and would hold the council responsible. She'd only learn new tools under instruction, preferring her father's notebook-and-pencil way.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The third is called AGI by 2028. Next one. The singularity hits fast. Within 2 years, by 2028, there is full AGI: artificial general intelligence, meaning AI that can do almost any work a person can do, as well or better, and cheaper. With robots it reaches hands-on work too. It arrives before most companies, governments and families have time to prepare. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say this is wrong, and the men who made it should answer for it. You don't throw a whole country's work away in two years. I'd say it at the mosque and at the yard, and I'd mean it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Off the record, I'd be finished at the department, I'm sure of it. I'm the newest and the slowest, and if the town can buy a machine that climbs, they will, even if they feel bad about it. And Idris fixes tractors, and if the tractors drive and fix themselves, that's both of us.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd cut everything that night, no holiday, no new clothes, no eating out. I'd sit down with my brothers and my mother and talk about how we help each other, maybe we'd share the big shop or the car. I wouldn't go to the government, I'd go to my family and the community first.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Frightened, honestly. Like the night Dad went into hospital.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: With only 2 years' warning, what would you do before it arrives?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Save every penny and pay down what we can on the house. There's no point me learning computers, not at my age and not in two years. I'd rather the house was closer to being ours.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you tell Yusuf and Maryam?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: That we're a family and families get through things. That God has a plan even when people make a mess. And that they need to work hard at school, because whatever comes, people who work hard find a way.

S2.say: This is wrong, and the people who made it should answer for it, because you don't throw a whole country's work away in two years. I'd say that at the mosque and at the yard.
S2.think: I'd be finished at the department, because I'm the newest and slowest and the town would buy a machine that climbs. Idris fixes tractors, and if tractors drive and fix themselves, that's both of us.
S2.do: Cuts holidays, clothes and eating out the night it's announced and pays down what she can on the house. Meets her brothers and mother to share costs like the weekly shop or a car, turning to family and community before government.
S2.feel: Frightened, like the night her father went into hospital.
S2.quote: I wouldn't go to the government, I'd go to my family and the community first.
S2.fieldNote: Her alarm comes from double exposure: her junior post and her husband's hands-on trade. She turns firmly to family, faith and community rather than state support, in line with her values. She sees no point retraining in two years.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The fourth is called AGI by 2031. Now the same thing, a bit slower. Full AGI arrives within 5 years, by 2031: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. There are a few years to see it coming, but it's still fast. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say the same as with the fast one, that it's wrong, but I'd say we've got time to stand up for ourselves. Towns like ours should keep control of their own lines and their own jobs. I'd go to the council meetings.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Five years, I'd be qualified, but still the newest qualified one. It might buy me some time, but in the end I think I'd still be out. I'm not going to pretend I'd become someone who programmes robots.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Finish my apprenticeship, keep paying extra off the mortgage, keep the savings growing. I'd tell Yusuf to look at nursing or something with people rather than a trade, which breaks my heart to say. And I'd go to every council meeting about the department.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Anxious. It sits in my stomach.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Telling Yusuf not to go into a trade breaks your heart. Why?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Because my family has always worked with its hands, Dad on the lines, my grandfather on the farm. I wanted Yusuf to be the third. But I won't send him into a trade that's about to vanish just for my pride.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What gets cut first if money gets tight in this one?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: The summer trip to see Idris's cousins, which is a long drive and costs a lot in fuel. Then I'd do more batch cooking, I was a school cook, I can feed five on very little. We'd manage.

S3.say: It's wrong, but with five years we have time to stand up for ourselves. Towns like ours should keep control of their own lines and jobs.
S3.think: In five years I'd be qualified but still the newest qualified one, so it might buy time but I'd still end up out. I won't pretend I'd become someone who programmes robots.
S3.do: Finishes her apprenticeship, keeps overpaying the mortgage and growing savings, and cuts the costly summer trip. Steers her son away from a trade toward people-focused work, and attends every council meeting about the department.
S3.feel: Anxious, a feeling that sits in her stomach.
S3.quote: I won't send him into a trade that's about to vanish just for my pride.
S3.fieldNote: The most painful moment was her steering her son away from the family tradition of working with his hands. Her political action is local: council meetings to keep the town's department. Five years buys her qualification but not much confidence.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: The last one is called AGI by 2036. Last one. Full AGI arrives within 10 years, by 2036: AI that can do almost any work a person can do, hands-on work included through robots. It's the same end point, but there's about a decade to prepare, change careers and make plans. If this happened, what would you say about it at work, to friends, or online?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: I'd say ten years gives us time to do it the right way, keeping families and towns in mind. I'd want apprenticeships kept going, not cut. I'd say it to anyone who'd listen.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: And just between us, off the record, what do you really think it means for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Ten years, I'd be 53, qualified for years, maybe with my name on the call-out list as a proper lineworker. That would mean a lot to me, to have done what Dad did. But I'd still worry about the end of it, I don't know what I'd do after.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: What would you actually do, starting now and in the first year after it arrives? Be as specific as you can.

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Keep going, qualify, and work as hard as I can for as long as they'll have me. Keep saving and paying the house down so it's nearly ours by the time it arrives. And help the kids into training that'll last, whatever that turns out to be.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: How does it feel, picturing that?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: Still anxious, but less. It's further away, but it's still coming.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Compared with 2 or 5 years, what does the decade change for you?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: It means I get to be a real lineworker, like Dad, for a good while. With two years I'm just the cook who tried. With ten, I've done it.

transcript.speaker: interviewer
transcript.text: Would the extra time change your mind about learning the new tools?

transcript.speaker: persona
transcript.text: No. I know that's stubborn. I'd rather spend those years being good at the old work than bad at the new.

S4.say: Ten years gives us time to do it the right way, keeping families and towns in mind. Apprenticeships should be kept going, not cut.
S4.think: In ten years I'd be 53 and a proper qualified lineworker on the call-out list, which would mean a lot because it's what Dad did. But I'd still worry about the end of it, and I don't know what I'd do after.
S4.do: Keeps going and qualifies, working as hard as she can for as long as she is kept on. Keeps saving and paying down the house so it's nearly theirs by the time it arrives, and helps her children into training that will last.
S4.feel: Still anxious, but less, because it's further away but still coming.
S4.quote: With two years I'm just the cook who tried. With ten, I've done it.
S4.fieldNote: The decade matters to her mainly because it lets her fulfil her father's trade. She stays anxious because she has no plan for after and won't learn new tools even with time. She chooses the old work done well over the new done badly.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Of the five pictures, which one worries you most, and what would actually help you if it happened?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: The two-year one, because Idris and I would both lose our work at once and I'd never finish what my dad started. What would help is keeping small departments like ours in the town's hands, keeping apprentices on, and not letting big companies from the city just buy everything up.

closing.speaker: interviewer
closing.text: Is there anything I didn't ask that I should have?

closing.speaker: persona
closing.text: You didn't ask why it matters who keeps the lines. When the power's out in a blizzard, people want to see a truck with the town's name on it and someone they know climbing the pole. A robot doesn't know whose grandmother is on oxygen.

headlineQuote: A robot doesn't know whose grandmother is on oxygen.
portrait: Jade Usman is a 43-year-old second-year apprentice at her small town's own electric department, a former school cook who took up the trade at 41 to follow her late father, a lineman of thirty-five years. She lives with her husband Idris, a tractor mechanic, their two children and a mortgage, with about three months of savings. She is traditional, guided by family and faith, refuses AI tools and turns to family and community before government. She is calm if AI stalls, uneasy about her department being merged in steady change, and alarmed by AGI in two years because both incomes would go. More time eases her only partly: it lets her finish her father's trade.
biggestWorry: AGI by 2028, because she and her husband would lose their work at once and she'd never finish what her father started.
whatWouldHelp: Keeping small departments in the town's hands, keeping apprentices on, and stopping big city companies from buying everything up.
